questions.text: Why does `fib` need two base cases, `fib(0)` and `fib(1)`?
options: `fib(n)` calls both `fib(n - 1)` and `fib(n - 2)`, so with only `fib(1)` a call would go past it to -1, -2...
Python needs every recursive function to have exactly two base cases
So that the function returns a list of two numbers
One is for even numbers and the other for odd numbers

questions.text: Why does the lesson call this `fib` not very efficient?
options: Because adding two numbers is slow in Python
Because it has two base cases instead of one
It works out the same values again and again: `fib(5)` and `fib(4)` both compute `fib(3)`
Because it builds a list of every number it finds
